one_liner: Smoke has no true binary boundary: model rankings on smoke benchmarks flip when evaluated against density (alpha) labels instead of binary masks.
problem: Smoke segmentation benchmarks use binary masks over a physically continuous density field; annotator thresholds are arbitrary, so benchmarks may rank annotator-style-matching, not smoke understanding.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: inter-annotator agreement on smoke binary masks is lower than model-model agreement (benchmarks measure style), and re-evaluating existing models against soft density references (from synthetic smoke composites with known alpha) produces materially different rankings.
why_important: If rankings are unstable under label formulation, published progress in smoke segmentation is partly an artifact - and safety systems are being selected on the wrong criterion.
why_possibly_novel: Density-referenced re-evaluation of binary smoke benchmarks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Composite real smoke plumes (alpha known from studio capture or simulation) onto scenes; evaluate public smoke models against binary vs alpha references; run a 5-annotator agreement study on 100 frames.
main_risk: Synthetic composites may not represent real smoke edge statistics; include a small real multi-annotator set.

one_liner: Reformulate smoke segmentation as alpha-matte regression: binary masks impose a measurable performance ceiling.
problem: Binary segmentation of translucent media discards the concentration information that downstream users (fire response, emissions monitoring) actually need.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a density-regression formulation trained on composited data with true alpha outperforms binary-mask models even when both are evaluated on the binary task (thresholded density beats direct binary prediction), because the continuous target regularizes the ill-posed boundary - falsifiable by direct comparison.
why_important: Would show binary supervision is not just lossy for users but actively harmful for learning on translucent classes.
why_possibly_novel: KNOWN: matting exists as a field; the claim that regression supervision dominates binary supervision ON the binary metric for smoke is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train matched models (same backbone/budget) with binary vs alpha supervision on composited smoke, evaluate both on binary IoU + downstream density error.
main_risk: Compositing realism gap; validate on held-out real annotated smoke.

one_liner: Fire segmentation models exploit sensor blooming and saturation artifacts, so they collapse across cameras: quantify the artifact reliance.
problem: Fire is a light emitter that saturates sensors, causing blooming/streaks that are camera-specific. Models may key on these artifacts rather than fire appearance, predicting cross-camera fragility.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: masking saturated pixels and blooming halos at test time degrades fire-segmentation models far more than masking equal-area random regions, and cross-camera transfer loss correlates with inter-camera differences in saturation behavior - most 'fire recognition' is sensor-artifact recognition.
why_important: Fire detection is deployed across wildly heterogeneous cameras; artifact reliance would explain field failures that benchmarks never show.
why_possibly_novel: Artifact-reliance decomposition for emissive phenomena is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Occlusion-based attribution on saturation regions across 3 fire datasets; cross-camera evaluation where saturation statistics are matched vs mismatched.
main_risk: Saturation is also genuine signal (fires do saturate); the question is reliance degree - needs careful counterfactuals with HDR captures.

one_liner: Fire flicker has a characteristic temporal frequency signature: a 1-second temporal window beats any single-frame architecture at matched compute.
problem: Flame combustion produces documented flicker (~1-15 Hz region, KNOWN from combustion literature). Whether video fire segmentation actually needs or uses this cue is untested against strong single-frame baselines.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: adding a short temporal window with explicit frequency-band features improves fire/no-fire pixel discrimination against hard negatives (sunsets, reflective orange surfaces, foliage in wind) more than scaling the single-frame model by the equivalent compute - temporal spectrum is the discriminative axis, not appearance.
why_important: Hard negatives are the practical fire-alarm problem (false positives); a physically-grounded cue that separates them is directly deployable.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-domain evaluation against curated hard negatives at matched compute is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Assemble hard-negative video set (sunsets, brake lights, reflections), compare single-frame vs temporal-spectral models at matched FLOPs.
main_risk: Camera compression may destroy flicker at typical bitrates - itself an important deployment finding.

one_liner: Smoke-vs-cloud/fog discrimination is context-borne, not appearance-borne: source-region occlusion collapses model accuracy.
problem: Smoke, cloud, and fog patches can be locally indistinguishable; humans disambiguate by source attribution (rising from a point) and context. What information models actually use is unknown.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: occluding the plume's source region (bottom of plume, fire location) reduces smoke-vs-cloud discrimination accuracy to near chance for current models, showing classification is source-context-based, while texture-only patches carry <20% of the decision information - a measurable information decomposition.
why_important: Determines minimum viable input context for wildfire early-warning crops/tiles - a deployed-system design constraint derived from science.
why_possibly_novel: Context-vs-texture information decomposition for atmospheric classes is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Patch-occlusion and crop-size sweeps on smoke/cloud datasets; report accuracy vs available context radius.
main_risk: Dataset biases (smoke images differ from cloud images in irrelevant ways) can inflate texture-only accuracy; control with matched-scene pairs.

one_liner: Optical-flow divergence detects smoke before appearance does: advection physics as a detection signal for incipient smoke.
problem: Early smoke is nearly transparent - appearance models fail at exactly the high-value moment. But smoke's motion field (expanding, buoyant, divergent) differs from scene motion from the very first frames.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: divergence/curl statistics of dense optical flow in smoke regions differ measurably from all common scene motions (foliage, water, crowds) even at contrast levels where appearance models are at chance, moving time-to-detection earlier by a measurable margin on ignition videos.
why_important: Time-to-detection is THE metric for wildfire monitoring; a physics-grounded earliness gain matters more than IoU gains.
why_possibly_novel: Flow-topology (divergence) statistics as an early smoke feature, evaluated on time-to-detect, is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: On ignition-time videos (controlled burns), plot detection latency of flow-based vs appearance-based signals at matched false-positive rates.
main_risk: Optical flow is noisy exactly at low contrast; may need long temporal integration that erodes the earliness advantage.

one_liner: Measure the annotator alpha-threshold distribution: at what transparency do humans stop labeling smoke, and how much benchmark variance does it explain?
problem: Every smoke/fog annotation implicitly chooses a transparency cutoff. The distribution of these cutoffs across annotators and datasets has never been measured, though it defines what the labels mean.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: annotator alpha cutoffs vary widely (roughly 2x range in implied alpha) across individuals and datasets, and this single scalar explains the majority of inter-dataset label inconsistency for translucent classes - cutting cross-dataset training gains when unharmonized.
why_important: Provides the missing calibration constant for merging translucent-class datasets, and a general method for auditing implicit label thresholds.
why_possibly_novel: Psychophysical measurement of implicit annotation thresholds is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Show annotators composited smoke with known alpha ramps, elicit boundaries, estimate individual cutoffs; compare dataset-level implied cutoffs via composite probes.
main_risk: Cutoffs may be context-dependent (background luminance), making the scalar model too simple - the richer model is still measurable.

one_liner: Synthetic-fog robustness does not transfer to real fog because real fog is heterogeneous: quantify the homogeneity gap.
problem: Fog robustness is benchmarked with homogeneous Koschmieder-model synthetic fog (KNOWN: standard in robustness suites). Real fog has patchiness, depth-correlated density, and scattering halos.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: models hardened on homogeneous synthetic fog gain little or nothing on real fog scenes (transfer coefficient <30%), and the residual failure correlates with fog spatial heterogeneity statistics - synthetic-fog benchmarks systematically overstate robustness progress.
why_important: Autonomous-driving robustness claims rest partly on synthetic corruption suites; a measured transfer coefficient recalibrates those claims.
why_possibly_novel: Direct synthetic-to-real fog transfer measurement for segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train/harden on synthetic fog ladders, evaluate on real foggy datasets (ACDC fog split), regress residual error on measured heterogeneity indices.
main_risk: Real-fog GT is limited; heterogeneity indices from single images are approximate.

one_liner: Background luminance flips smoke difficulty: dark-smoke-on-sky vs light-smoke-on-ground asymmetry as an untested dataset bias.
problem: Smoke visibility depends on the sign of contrast with background (scattering vs shadowing regimes). Datasets may over-sample one regime, biasing models trained on them.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: public smoke datasets are dominated by positive-contrast configurations (bright smoke against dark ground or dark smoke against bright sky in fixed proportions), and model performance collapses on the under-represented contrast-sign regime - a bias measurable and correctable via regime-stratified evaluation.
why_important: Wildfire cameras see both regimes daily (sun angle changes); a hidden regime bias means diurnal reliability swings in deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Contrast-sign regime analysis for translucent classes is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Auto-classify contrast regimes in 4 smoke datasets, report regime distributions and per-regime model performance.
main_risk: Regime auto-classification itself needs validation; start with manual labeling of a subset.

one_liner: Smoke shadows are systematically mislabeled as smoke in aerial datasets: an audit with atmospheric-geometry verification.
problem: From aerial/satellite view, dense smoke casts dark shadows displaced by sun angle; annotators plausibly include shadows in smoke masks. Nobody has audited for this confusion.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a geometrically verifiable fraction (sun-angle-consistent displacement) of 'smoke' pixels in public aerial smoke datasets are actually shadow, and models trained on them systematically over-segment in the shadow direction - a directional error signature reproducible from sun metadata.
why_important: Burned-area and plume-volume estimates feed emissions science; a shadow contamination bias propagates into climate-relevant numbers.
why_possibly_novel: Sun-geometry forensic auditing of smoke annotations is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: For datasets with timestamps/geolocation, compute sun vectors, test whether label boundaries show sun-aligned asymmetry vs plume physics.
main_risk: Smoke and its shadow genuinely overlap when viewed off-nadir; geometry must handle view angle carefully.

one_liner: Rain streak and snowflake segmentation depends on exposure time, not weather intensity: the shutter-speed confound in weather datasets.
problem: The image of falling precipitation is determined jointly by physical rate and camera shutter speed (streak length ~ exposure). Datasets ignore shutter metadata, confounding weather severity with camera settings.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: model performance and even class definition ('rain streak' vs 'rain fog') vary more with exposure-time differences than with actual precipitation-rate differences at matched rates - weather segmentation datasets encode camera physics as much as meteorology.
why_important: Weather robustness claims should transfer across cameras; if not, deployed reliability varies with shutter policies (auto-exposure), a controllable but ignored factor.
why_possibly_novel: Exposure-time-controlled analysis of precipitation appearance in segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Capture matched scenes at multiple shutter speeds under controlled sprinkler 'rain'; test models across shutter conditions.
main_risk: Controlled precipitation capture is logistically heavy; simulation (streak rendering with exposure models) can substitute initially.

one_liner: Models segment reflections on water as if they were the reflected objects: quantify the reflection-confusion rate and its structure.
problem: Water surfaces mirror the scene; segmentation models may label reflected trees/people as real ones. The error rate and its dependence on water roughness is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: on calm-water scenes, mainstream models assign real-object classes to reflection pixels at high rates, and the confusion rate drops sharply with surface ripple amplitude (a measurable psychometric-style curve) - revealing that reflection rejection is driven by high-frequency distortion cues, not scene reasoning.
why_important: Waterside deployment (drones, boats, flood monitoring) needs reflection rejection; knowing the operative cue tells us when it fails (calm dawn water = worst case).
why_possibly_novel: Ripple-amplitude-controlled reflection confusion curves are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Curate calm-to-rippled water scene ladder, measure per-class confusion into reflection regions across models.
main_risk: GT for 'reflection region' needs annotation, but polygon-level water masks make it tractable.

one_liner: Steam vs smoke as the minimal-pair discrimination task for translucent media: what cue actually separates them?
problem: Steam (condensed water) and smoke (combustion aerosol) look similar but have different dynamics, color temperature, and dissipation. Alarm systems must separate them; the discriminative cue set is unknown.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: the separating information is temporal (dissipation rate, buoyancy profile) rather than static appearance - static-frame classifiers plateau near chance-plus-context, while short-clip models separate well; and the temporal advantage survives across cameras (unlike appearance cues).
why_important: False alarms from steam are a leading cause of fire-system distrust in kitchens/industry; a validated minimal cue set enables robust designs.
why_possibly_novel: Steam-smoke minimal-pair benchmark with cue ablation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Collect matched steam/smoke clips (kitchen + controlled sources), run static vs temporal models, ablate color/motion/context channels.
main_risk: Collection diversity (steam types vs smoke types) drives conclusions; needs deliberate source variety.

one_liner: Exposure bracketing beats model scaling for fire scenes: sensor dynamic range, not model capacity, is the current bottleneck.
problem: Fire scenes span extreme dynamic range (flame core to dark smoke); single-exposure images clip both ends. The community scales models on clipped data instead of asking whether the sensor is the binding constraint.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: at matched total cost, adding exposure-bracketed/HDR input to a small model outperforms scaling a single-exposure model by 10x parameters on fire-region segmentation and near-fire structure delineation - the information is destroyed before the model, and no capacity recovers clipped photons.
why_important: Would redirect investment from model scale toward capture policy for safety-critical fire perception - a cheap, actionable systems conclusion.
why_possibly_novel: Sensor-vs-model marginal-value comparison for fire segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Capture bracketed fire footage (controlled burns), train matched models on single vs bracketed inputs, compare against a parameter-scaling ladder.
main_risk: HDR capture is unavailable on legacy deployed cameras, limiting immediate applicability (but informing procurement).

one_liner: Time-to-detect as the primary smoke metric: temporal-accumulation detectors dominate spatial models in the sub-visible regime.
problem: Smoke benchmarks report IoU on established plumes; the deployment task is detecting the transition from nothing to barely-something, which is a change-detection problem, not a segmentation problem.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: on ignition sequences, simple long-horizon temporal accumulation (background modeling over minutes) detects smoke minutes earlier than frame-wise segmentation models at equal false-alarm rates - the field is optimizing the wrong problem formulation for the highest-value use case.
why_important: Minutes of earliness in wildfire detection have enormous real value; showing the formulation (not the model) is wrong would redirect the subfield.
why_possibly_novel: Ignition-anchored time-to-detect benchmarking of segmentation models is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Assemble ignition-timestamped fixed-camera videos (controlled burns, tower cameras), compare detection-latency ROC of accumulation vs segmentation approaches.
main_risk: Fixed-camera assumption; moving-camera earliness is a different, harder problem.

one_liner: IoU is the wrong loss surface for amorphous regions: measure human-judgment vs IoU ranking disagreement on smoke/fog masks.
problem: For amorphous media, many different masks are equally 'right'. Whether IoU-style metrics agree with expert human quality judgments on such classes has not been tested.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: for smoke/fog masks, human expert pairwise preferences disagree with IoU-based rankings on a large fraction of comparisons (>30%), and the disagreement is systematic (humans forgive boundary variation but punish topology/coverage errors) - implying a validated perceptual metric would reorder the field's results.
why_important: Metric validity precedes all benchmarking; a documented human-metric divergence forces metric reform for a whole class family.
why_possibly_novel: Human-preference validation of segmentation metrics for amorphous classes is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Collect 1k expert pairwise preferences over model masks on smoke scenes; fit which metric family predicts preferences.
main_risk: Expert preference may be application-dependent (emissions vs alarm); collect per-use-case preferences.

one_liner: Layered translucency compositions (smoke behind glass, fog over water) break single-layer models: a compositional generalization test for translucent classes.
problem: Datasets contain single translucent phenomena; reality composes them (smoke seen through a window). Whether models generalize compositionally to stacked translucency is untested.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: models trained on isolated smoke and isolated glass fail on their composition at rates far exceeding the product of individual error rates (super-multiplicative failure), demonstrating absence of compositional structure in learned translucency representations.
why_important: Compositional failure modes are silent in standard evaluation but common in deployment (indoor fires seen through windows are THE fire-alarm case).
why_possibly_novel: Compositional stress testing for translucent phenomena is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Composite controlled stacks (real captures through glass with/without smoke machine), evaluate single-phenomenon models on compositions.
main_risk: Physical capture effort; partial substitution with principled rendering possible.

one_liner: Is fire scale-invariant for segmentation? Test transfer from candle to wildfire along a pure scale ladder.
problem: Flames are quasi-fractal; if their image statistics are scale-invariant, small-fire data (cheap, safe to collect) should train large-fire models. Nobody has measured the transfer curve along scale.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: fire-region segmentation transfers across ~2 orders of magnitude of physical scale with <10% relative loss (supporting scale-invariance), but smoke does NOT (buoyancy regime changes plume morphology qualitatively) - a clean split between the two phenomena's scaling behavior.
why_important: Data-collection economics: if candle/bonfire data trains wildfire models, safe cheap data replaces dangerous expensive data.
why_possibly_novel: Scale-transfer curves for combustion phenomena are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Assemble scale-ladder dataset (candle, campfire, bonfire, controlled burn, wildfire footage), train at one scale, test across the ladder.
main_risk: Scale confounds with camera distance/atmosphere; normalize by apparent size and control compression.

one_liner: What matters in synthetic smoke: factor-ablate density-field realism vs lighting realism vs background realism for sim2real transfer.
problem: Fluid-simulated smoke is a promising data source, but rendering has many realism axes and nobody knows which one pays. Teams max out all axes at great cost.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: transfer performance is dominated by illumination/scattering realism (single-vs-multi-scatter, correct sun/sky) with density-field fidelity (simulation resolution) contributing little beyond coarse plume shape - i.e. cheap simulations with expensive lighting beat the reverse at matched render budget.
why_important: Defines the cost-optimal synthetic data recipe for all translucent media, transferable to fog/steam/dust.
why_possibly_novel: Factorial realism ablation for participating-media training data is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: 2x2x2 factorial render (density res x scattering model x background source), train per cell, evaluate on real smoke benchmarks.
main_risk: Interaction effects may defeat the factorial simplification; the design still detects them.

one_liner: Smoke motion vs camera motion entanglement in aerial footage: drone ego-motion masquerades as plume dynamics and vice versa.
problem: Drone-based wildfire monitoring adds ego-motion that corrupts the temporal cues (drift, divergence) that smoke detection depends on; how much of temporal-model advantage survives ego-motion is unknown.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: the accuracy advantage of temporal smoke models over static ones disappears almost entirely under drone ego-motion unless flow is ego-compensated, and compensation via cheap homography recovers most (not all) of it - the residual loss localizes to parallax-heavy terrain.
why_important: Quantifies exactly what stabilization/compensation infrastructure aerial fire systems need, and where terrain will still defeat them.
why_possibly_novel: Ego-motion ablation for temporal smoke cues is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Take fixed-camera smoke videos, synthetically inject ego-motion (crop-path animation), measure temporal-model degradation with/without compensation.
main_risk: Synthetic ego-motion lacks true parallax; complement with real paired drone/tower footage if available.

one_liner: Cloud-shadow vs smoke-plume confusion in satellite imagery: which spectral bands are actually load-bearing?
problem: Satellite smoke products confuse smoke with cloud shadows and haze. Band-importance for this specific confusion (not general segmentation) is unquantified in modern learned models.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: the smoke-vs-shadow decision in learned models rests almost entirely on 1-2 SWIR bands, and models degrade to near chance on this confusion pair when those bands are ablated - making sensor-band availability (differs across satellites) the primary cross-satellite transfer factor, above resolution.
why_important: Cross-satellite model reuse is constrained by band sets; knowing the load-bearing bands turns transfer failure from mystery to checklist.
why_possibly_novel: Confusion-pair-specific band attribution is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Band-ablation study on Sentinel/Landsat smoke datasets, scored specifically on smoke-vs-shadow confusion subsets.
main_risk: Band ablation in-model differs from retraining without the band; do both for the key bands.

one_liner: Heat shimmer (refractive turbulence) as a segmentable phenomenon: detecting invisible hot-air regions from background distortion alone.
problem: Hot air above fires/engines/roads is invisible in RGB appearance but visibly distorts the background. No benchmark or method targets refractive-media segmentation, though it precedes visible flame/smoke.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: temporal distortion statistics (local nonrigid displacement variance with characteristic frequency) suffice to segment shimmer regions with useful IoU on fixed cameras, and shimmer onset precedes visible smoke in a measurable fraction of ignition videos - a genuinely new early-fire channel.
why_important: Adds a new physical channel to early fire detection and defines a novel task class (segmenting media visible only through their distortion field).
why_possibly_novel: Refractive-region segmentation as a task is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (Schlieren imaging is KNOWN but requires special optics; this is passive RGB).
minimal_experiment: Collect fixed-camera footage over heat sources, compute distortion-field features, label shimmer regions, benchmark simple classifiers; check shimmer-before-smoke timing on ignition clips.
main_risk: Wind and camera vibration create confusable distortions; needs vibration controls.

one_liner: Koschmieder-law self-supervision: single-image fog density fields learnable from depth-luminance coupling without any fog labels.
problem: Fog density estimation lacks labels almost entirely. But atmospheric physics (KNOWN: Koschmieder attenuation model) couples scene depth, luminance shift, and fog density in a testable way that could supervise itself.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: enforcing consistency between a monocular depth estimate and the physically-implied luminance attenuation yields per-pixel fog-density maps that correlate strongly with transmissometer/visibility ground truth - label-free fog quantification from ordinary cameras.
why_important: Every traffic/airport camera becomes a visibility sensor; also provides dense fog supervision for downstream robustness training.
why_possibly_novel: KNOWN: dehazing uses these physics; closing the loop as self-supervised density REGRESSION validated against meteorological ground truth is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Use webcam archives near airports (with METAR visibility records), fit the self-supervised model, validate against recorded visibility.
main_risk: Depth estimators are themselves fog-sensitive - circularity must be broken with clear-day depth priors of fixed scenes.

one_liner: Auto-exposure dynamics leak global fire evidence: models 'detect' fire from image-wide brightness adaptation, not fire pixels.
problem: When a camera auto-exposes to a bright flame, the whole image changes. Models may exploit this global cue, inflating benchmark scores and failing on manually-exposed or HDR cameras.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: fire-classification/segmentation models retain substantial accuracy when fire pixels are fully masked (evidence of global-cue reliance), and this reliance predicts their failure rate on constant-exposure footage - a shortcut with a measurable deployment cost.
why_important: Shortcut detection with direct deployment implications; also a general warning for any emissive-target dataset collected with auto-exposure cameras.
why_possibly_novel: Auto-exposure shortcut analysis is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Mask fire regions on test sets, measure retained accuracy; compare model performance on auto- vs fixed-exposure paired captures.
main_risk: Masked-region inpainting artifacts can themselves leak information; use multiple masking strategies.

one_liner: Deduplicate smoke/fire benchmarks by video provenance: same-event frames in train and test inflate scores, and rankings change after cleanup.
problem: Smoke/fire datasets are assembled from scraped videos; frames of the same event often land in both train and test splits, making benchmarks partially a memorization test.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: provenance-level deduplication (event/video-level splits) drops reported performance substantially (>10 points for some methods) and reorders methods, with the biggest drops for highest-capacity models - current smoke/fire SOTA is partly leakage measurement.
why_important: Safety-critical procurement decisions cite these benchmarks; leakage-corrected numbers are the ones that predict field performance.
why_possibly_novel: Provenance-forensic re-splitting of fire/smoke benchmarks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (leakage audits in other domains are KNOWN).
minimal_experiment: Perceptual-hash + temporal correlation clustering across 4 public datasets to find leaked pairs; re-evaluate public models on clean splits.
main_risk: Aggressive dedup may over-merge distinct-but-similar events; manual verification of clusters needed.
